title: Project Progress Log
text:
Week 1 : Backend Architecture, Simulation Engine, and AWS Integration
The first week of the project focused on establishing the foundational architecture required for a real-time logistics simulation platform. We began by defining the overall system design, outlining a pipeline that connects a FastAPI backend simulation engine to an AWS DynamoDB database for persistent storage, and finally to a browser-based frontend powered by Leaflet.js and WebSockets. Once the architecture was set, we implemented the core backend simulation engine using FastAPI and asyncio. This included building the /start-sim endpoint to initialize trips, a WebSocket endpoint for streaming updates to the frontend, and helper modules for routing, geospatial calculations, and time estimation. The simulation logic for both trucks and ships was developed, since trucks follow realistic polyline paths obtained from the OSRM routing API, and ships follow stochastic movements near Basra Port to represent maritime activity.
A major achievement in Week 1 was integrating AWS DynamoDB as the persistent storage layer. We organized the database to store truck states, ship states, route polylines, cumulative distance calculations, and metadata such as ETAs. We implemented serialization/deserialization helpers using Python’s Decimal type to satisfy DynamoDB’s type system to handle all the errors. Complex logic by the help of LLMs was added to reset simulation state safely using paginated Scan and Delete operations. By the end of the week, the backend was capable of generating realistic simulations, storing data in the cloud, and maintaining consistent state across iterations. This helped lay the foundation for the rest of our project.


Week 2 : Frontend Development, Deployment, and System Stabilization
Week 2 transitioned into building and refining the user-facing portion of the project. Using Leaflet.js, we implemented an interactive geospatial map capable of rendering trucks, ships, and routes in real time. Custom icons, popups with metadata, route polylines, and dynamic camera fitting were added to create a polished and intuitive interface. The frontend was connected to the backend WebSocket stream, allowing truck and ship locations to update every second. We also added UI enhancements, such as updated status labels, ETAs, progress tracking, and depot markers.
In parallel, we focused on deployment and system reliability. The backend was containerized and deployed to Fly.io, requiring modifications to ensure that FastAPI listened on the correct port (0.0.0.0:8080) and that environment variables for AWS access were properly handled. We also deployed the frontend as a static Quarto website to cPanel, updating JavaScript paths and WebSocket URLs for production. During Week 2, significant debugging was performed to resolve issues such as WebSocket disconnections, CORS restrictions, stale cached JavaScript files, and DynamoDB item type inconsistencies. By the end of the week, the system was fully integrated end-to-end: the frontend map could start a simulation, the backend could generate and update real-time data, and the database accurately stored and streamed operational states.


Week 3 : Machine Learning Integration, Evaluation, and Final Documentation
The third week focused on improving the simulation with machine learning and preparing the full analytical and technical documentation. We implemented both unsupervised and supervised learning components as per the project requirement. For unsupervised learning, we created a KMeans clustering model trained on simulated operational features such as planned speed and remaining distance. The model grouped trucks into clusters representing fast, slow, and anomalous behavior patterns. For supervised learning, we generated a labeled dataset and trained a logistic regression model to estimate delay probability based on key trip characteristics. Both models were exported as .pkl files and integrated into the backend pipeline, allowing real-time inference inside the simulation loop. The frontend was updated to display each truck’s cluster assignment and delay risk percentage, completing the ML-enhanced monitoring system.
Significant effort in Week 3 was also devoted to debugging ML deployment issues, including dependency mismatches involving NumPy and scikit-learn. Many of the models and fly.io could work on older versions of the libraries. After resolving these issues and rebuilding the deployment image, the system began successfully generating real-time ML predictions. The final portion of the week was spent writing the technical report sections: data collection, data cleaning, EDA, unsupervised learning, supervised learning, system design, and implementation details.

title: Debugging Guide - Trucks Not Showing on Map
text:
I’ve added comprehensive debugging to help identify the issue. Follow these steps:


When you start the server, you should see:
🔗 Connected to DynamoDB table 'Shipments' in region 'eu-north-1'
When you click “Start Simulation”, look for:
[START] Simulation started with X trucks from Origin to Destination
[SIM] Starting simulation loop...
[SIM] First payload: X trucks, Y ships
[SIM] Connected clients: 1
[SIM] Sent initial payload to client
What to check: - Are trucks being created? Look for the count in the log - Are clients connected? Should be at least 1 - Any error messages?



Open your browser’s Developer Tools (F12) and check the Console tab.
Expected logs:
[WS] Attempting to connect to ws://localhost:8000/ws
[WS] ✅ Connected to ws://localhost:8000/ws
[WS] 📨 Received message
[WS] Data - Trucks: 4 Ships: 2 Route points: 200
[MAP] Processing 4 trucks
[MAP] ➕ Creating marker for TRUCK-1 at 30.5081 47.7835
What to check: - Is WebSocket connected? If not, check if server is running - Are trucks in the data? Look for the count - Are markers being created?





Symptoms: Console shows [WS] ❌ Error or connection fails Solution: - Make sure server is running: uvicorn server:app --reload --port 8000 - Check if port 8000 is available - If using file:// protocol, start a local server instead



Symptoms: Console shows [WS] Data - Trucks: 0 Ships: X Solution: - Check backend logs - are trucks being created in DynamoDB? - Verify DynamoDB table exists and is accessible - Check AWS credentials



Symptoms: Console shows trucks but no markers Solution: - Check for JavaScript errors in console - Verify truck coordinates are valid numbers - Check if Leaflet map is initialized (zoom to see if map loads)



Symptoms: No logs after initial connection Solution: - The simulation loop should start automatically when you click “Start Simulation” - Check backend logs for errors in simulation_loop() - Verify the /start-sim endpoint was called successfully




Test the endpoints directly:
# Test if server is running
curl http://localhost:8000/

# Test start simulation
curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/start-sim \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"numTrucks": 2, "origin": "Basra Port", "destination": "Baghdad Depot", "departure": "2024-01-01T00:00:00"}'



Verify data is actually in DynamoDB:
# List all items with TRUCK prefix
aws dynamodb scan \
  --table-name Shipments \
  --filter-expression "begins_with(truckId, :prefix)" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":prefix":{"S":"TRUCK-"}}' \
  --region eu-north-1
You should see trucks with IDs like TRUCK-1, TRUCK-2, etc.



If trucks still don’t show up: 1. Share the backend server logs 2. Share the browser console output 3. Check if there are any JavaScript errors in the console
The debugging output will help identify exactly where the issue is!

title: Unsupervised Learning
text: ```markdown

title: Unsupervised Learning
text: title: “Unsupervised Learning”

title: Unsupervised Learning
section: Introduction to Unsupervised Learning in the Logistics Simulation
text:
Introduction to Unsupervised Learning in the Logistics Simulation
Unsupervised learning helps spot new behavior trends in our simulated logistics setup - using live data instead of pre-labeled results. As the simulation produces constant updates like vehicle speed, location, distance covered, or task completion rates, this method reveals hidden organization in fast-moving streams of detailed information. It’s key for noticing when trips differ from norms, recognizing unusual motion sequences, while grouping vehicles based on how they perform. In our work, it supports ongoing tracking of fleets and improves later predictive systems by adding subtle but useful data cues.

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Clustering Objective and Rationale
The goal here is grouping trucks by how they operate throughout a trip. Although every truck moves along the same set path between start and end points, their behaviors aren’t identical - expected speeds change according to OSRM time predictions, left-over distances shift unevenly due to differing departure times, while outside factors like rerouting or minor delays add further differences.
Clustering these operational characteristics helps us answer several important logistical questions:

Which trucks are progressing unusually slowly or quickly?
Are there natural groupings of vehicles based on route difficulty or distance remaining?
Can we detect potential anomalies early by comparing a truck’s behavior to its cluster peers?
How do operational factors naturally segment across different routes?

Unsupervised segmentation provides actionable insights even in a simulated setting, aligning closely with industry fleet-monitoring practices.

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Clustering Methodology: K-Means
We employ K-Means clustering, a widely used algorithm for partitioning numerical data into k distinct groups based on similarity.
Training procedure: A dataset of simulated truck journeys was collected across multiple routes.
For each logged timestamp, planned_speed_kmh and dist_remaining_km were extracted.
The data was normalized (if necessary) to stabilize cluster boundaries.
K-Means was fit with k = 3, producing the following conceptual clusters:








Cluster
Interpretation
Behavioral Pattern




0 – Long-Distance / Early Journey
High remaining distance, moderate speed
Truck has just begun its route


1 – Mid-Route / Steady State
Moderate distance remaining
Most trucks spend the longest time here


2 – Arrival Phase / Low Distance
Nearly complete
Truck is close to the depot and progress stabilizes

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Real-Time Application in the Simulation
Once deployed, the trained model is loaded by the backend and applied to each truck every simulation tick:
cluster = kmeans_model.predict([[plan_speed_kmh, dist_remaining]])[0] The assigned cluster is then included in the WebSocket payload and displayed on the frontend map inside each truck’s information popup.
This enables: Live monitoring of fleet behavior

Pattern detection (e.g., which clusters appear most often)
Quick visual segmentation of trucks along the route
Future anomaly detection (trucks behaving differently from cluster peers)

Even though this is a simulated environment, the clustering system behaves exactly like one used in real-world fleet analytics.

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Insights Gained from Clustering
During EDA and deployment, clustering revealed several useful insights:

Trucks with longer or more complex OSRM routes tend to fall into higher-distance clusters early on.
Variability in planned speed often creates distinct cluster boundaries even when trucks are the same distance from the destination.
The cluster IDs provide a simple but effective indicator of operational phase: beginning, middle, or near completion.
These cluster features became important inputs to subsequent supervised models (e.g., predicting delay risk).

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Limitations and Considerations
While K-Means is simple and effective, several limitations need to be acknowledged:

Clusters are spherical and may not capture nonlinear route behaviors.
Synthetic data reduces variability, which can make clusters appear cleaner than in reality.
The model must be retrained if new features are introduced or if simulation behavior changes drastically.
Scaling issues may arise if the feature magnitudes differ significantly.

In future extensions, more advanced unsupervised methods—such as DBSCAN for anomaly detection or Gaussian Mixture Models for probabilistic segmentation—could enrich system insights.

title: Unsupervised Learning
text:
Conclusion
Using unsupervised methods helped uncover hidden patterns in the simulated delivery data. Because trucks were grouped by target speed and left-over distance, insights became clearer during live operation. Such grouping links actual simulation output with later prediction models that rely on labeled examples.

title: Data Collection
text:
This project skips outside data sources altogether - rather, it builds its own made-up stream of logistics events that mirror cargo flows through Iraq. Its aim is to craft a repeatable flow of location-tagged records updated fast enough for live tracking, pattern spotting without labels, training models with examples, or predicting daily operations.
All created data flows straight into AWS DynamoDB, where it’s saved and later pulled from; this database runs the show for analysis, visuals, or training smart systems. Everything works through code. This way, each phase starting from making events up to saving and grabbing them back, can be repeated exactly when needed.



All simulation info comes from a Python event engine (server.py), then lands in an AWS DynamoDB table named Shipments - this holds everything live. Instead of just saving records, it keeps trucks, vessels, paths, total miles, forecast feautures, pand all other active simulation entities; at the same time, it streams updates to a WebSocket-powered front end and feeds traits into ML guesses like KMeans groups delay-risk predictions. It runs on DynamoDB inside eu-north-1, sorting entries by truckId up top. Several types of synthetic data are produced by the simulation layer, including truck movement events created by stepping through OSRM-generated routes, ship movement events based on random GPS jitter, full polyline route geometries obtained through the OSRM API, cumulative distance profiles computed using the haversine formula, and machine learning features such as delay probabilities generated by pretrained sklearn models. The only external data dependency is the Open Source Routing Machine (OSRM) API, which provides realistic drivable routes in Iraq by returning full road polylines, true route lengths, and geometry needed for accurate ETA estimation.



The project does not scrape or fetch static datasets. Instead, it implements a real-time streaming data generator that emits events every second.


When the user clicks Start Simulation, the backend:

Reads user parameters


Number of trucks
Origin hub
Destination hub
Departure time


Computes optimal route Calls OSRM to obtain:


Polyline coordinates
Total route length
Estimated travel duration


Initializes all trucks Each truck is saved to DynamoDB with:


truckId
start, end
lat, lon
route (full polyline, serialized for DynamoDB)
cumdist (cumulative distance array)
total_km
idx (route pointer)
ETA, status, etc.


Starts the streaming simulation loop Every second:


Trucks advance along the route polyline
Ships drift randomly
ML inference is computed (cluster + delay risk)
All updates are written to DynamoDB

Updated state is broadcast to the frontend via WebSocket (/ws)




FastAPI — backend server + WebSocket streaming
boto3 — DynamoDB read/write operations
requests — OSRM routing calls
asyncio — high-frequency simulation loop
joblib — loading ML models

All data collection logic exists in server.py, ensuring full reproducibility.




Every record stored in DynamoDB follows a consistent JSON-serializable schema. Example truck record:
{ “truckId”: “TRUCK-1”, “start”: “Basra Port”, “end”: “Baghdad Depot”, “lat”: 31.2044, “lon”: 46.8091, “route”: [ {“lat”: 30.5081, “lon”: 47.7835}, {“lat”: 30.61, “lon”: 47.12}, … ], “cumdist”: [0, 1.2, 2.8, …], “total_km”: 545.3, “idx”: 42, “eta”: “2025-12-10T19:50:00Z”, “status”: “IN_TRANSIT”, “plan_speed_kmh”: 78.2, “cluster”: 1, “delayRisk”: 0.32 }
Data Formats used:



Component
Format




Truck and ship data
JSON records stored in DynamoDB


Route geometry
GeoJSON from OSRM, stored as list of points


WebSocket packets
JSON


ML models
.pkl (joblib)









The entire pipeline, from event generation to machine learning inference, is fully open, deterministic, and well-documented, ensuring complete transparency throughout the system. The use of synthetic yet realistic simulation logic, deterministic routing from OSRM, traceable event updates, reproducible ML inference via static .pkl models, and publicly accessible backend, frontend, and ML code allows every step of the workflow to be replicated without ambiguity. This means that anyone can reproduce the simulation logic, rebuild the DynamoDB dataset, rerun the clustering and delay risk models, and recreate the live geospatial visualizations exactly as demonstrated. Together, these elements satisfy all requirements for reproducibility and open technical methodology.

title: Supervised Learning
text: ```markdown

title: Supervised Learning
text: title: “Supervised Learning”

title: Supervised Learning
section: Introduction to Supervised Learning in the Simulation System
text:
Introduction to Supervised Learning in the Simulation System
Supervised learning drives predictions in our logistics simulation. Although clustering uncovers hidden patterns and phases across truck activities, prediction relies on past data to estimate what might happen next. Real-world logistics uses forecasting to spot delays, identify problems early, improve resource use, or act ahead of disruptions. To mirror this behavior, the system applies a classification method that judges how likely a truck is to face major delays given its current status.
Introducing a guided prediction feature shifts the simulation beyond basic visual output, turning it into a practical aid for choices - showing how algorithms boost supply planning using modeled information instead of real inputs.

title: Supervised Learning
section: Defining the Prediction Task: Delay Risk Classification
text:
Defining the Prediction Task: Delay Risk Classification
The supervised learning task focuses on predicting delay risk, defined as the likelihood that a truck will arrive substantially later than its OSRM-estimated arrival time.
Target Variable (Label) We constructed a binary target variable, is_delayed, where:

0 = Truck arrived on time or early
1 = Truck arrived late beyond a threshold (e.g., ≥ 15% over OSRM ETA)

Because real-world delay labels do not exist in a simulation, we generated labeled data by running multiple simulated journeys and computing actual arrival times versus expected arrival times. This mirrors how organizations bootstrap internal prediction systems without full historical records.

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Training Dataset Construction
To train the supervised model, we generated a dataset consisting of simulated truck journeys running across multiple city pairs with randomized offsets, different OSRM route geometries, and varying average speeds. For each truck, the following features were captured at the beginning of the journey:
Input Features | Feature | Description | Why It Matters | |———————–|———————————————————–|———————————————————————————-| | Planned Speed (km/h) | Estimated from OSRM travel time and distance | Lower planned speeds correlate with difficult routes such as mountainous or urban regions | | Distance Remaining (km) | Total kilometers left in the journey at prediction time | Longer routes naturally carry higher uncertainty and increased delay probability | | Stops Feature | Count of simulated mid-route stops (set to 0 in baseline) | Placeholder for future enhancements such as port bottlenecks or roadblocks |

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Model Choice: Logistic Regression
We selected Logistic Regression as the primary classifier for delay prediction. The model offers several advantages suitable for simulation-based predictive analytics:

Highly interpretable coefficients
Efficient to train and very lightweight, enabling microsecond-level inference
Robust baseline for probabilistic classification
Well-suited to binary delay vs. non-delay outcomes

Although more complex algorithms (e.g., Random Forests, Gradient Boosting) could offer marginal accuracy improvements, Logistic Regression aligns best with our goals of transparency, speed, and ease of integration with the backend.

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Training Procedure

Data generation Multiple runs of the simulation produced a training corpus of journeys with real arrival times and predicted arrival times.
Feature engineering Numerical features were standardized, and the target variable was computed.
Train/test split 80% of examples were used for training; 20% for testing.
Model training Logistic Regression was fit using scikit-learn:

model = LogisticRegression() model.fit(X_train, y_train)

Evaluation metrics We evaluated performance using:


Accuracy
Precision & Recall
ROC–AUC
Confusion Matrix

These metrics quantify how well the model distinguishes between on-time vs. delayed trips.

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Model Deployment and Integration
After training, the supervised model was serialized using joblib and deployed inside the backend server’s /models directory:
delay_model = joblib.load(“models/delay_model.pkl”) During each simulation update cycle, the backend computes real-time features:

plan_speed_kmh
dist_remaining
stops_feature (currently 0)

Then it performs inference:
proba = delay_model.predict_proba([[plan_speed_kmh, dist_remaining, stops_feature]])[0] delay_risk = float(proba[1]) This delayRisk value is added to the WebSocket payload alongside cluster ID and real-time positions.

title: Supervised Learning
section: Real-Time Application in the Live Simulation
text:
Real-Time Application in the Live Simulation
The supervised model allows the logistics map to display dynamic, predictive insights for every active truck:

Each truck marker popup shows “Delay Risk: XX.X%”
Higher probabilities indicate that the truck is statistically more likely to arrive behind schedule
Operators can visually scan the fleet for trucks posing elevated risk
Combined with cluster assignment, the system provides both descriptive (cluster) and predictive (risk) intelligence in real time

This mirrors modern predictive logistics systems used by Amazon, DHL, Maersk, and UPS, where ML is embedded directly into operational dashboards.

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Interpretation and Business Relevance
Although the supervised model uses simulated labels, the approach reflects widely adopted practices in supply-chain intelligence:

Predictive delay modeling helps allocate resources proactively
Early warning allows for dynamic rerouting or dispatching backup vehicles
Risk predictions improve reliability and customer satisfaction
Provides a scalable foundation for adding more sophisticated ML models later

In our project, the model not only enhances realism but also demonstrates how machine learning integrates into real-time operational decision systems.

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Limitations and Future Extensions

Because the training labels come from simulations, the model is only as realistic as the assumptions underlying the simulation.
Additional features (traffic, weather, congestion, road type) would improve predictive fidelity.
The current stops_feature is a placeholder; implementing real bottlenecks would produce richer patterns.
More advanced models (Random Forests, Gradient Boosted Trees, Neural Nets) could capture nonlinear relationships.

Despite these limitations, the current system provides a robust foundation that illustrates the value of supervised analytics in a logistics context.

title: Supervised Learning
text:
Conclusion
The supervised learning component transforms the project from a simple visualization of moving trucks into an intelligent system capable of forecasting operational risks. By predicting delay probabilities in real time, the system showcases how machine learning can meaningfully enhance situational awareness and decision-making in logistics—whether in a simulated environment or a real-world supply chain.

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text: title: “Data Cleaning”

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text:
Introduction to Data Cleaning
The data cleaning step is key to getting our simulated logistics info ready for exploration, modeling, or live visuals. Although we create fake events instead of pulling outside data, the stream setup still brings familiar issues, like mismatched layouts, blank entries, broken location points, or timing gaps. So cleanup turns into a repeating task, adjusting as simulations change, fresh ML traits appear, while analysis targets move. During building, this clean-up flow got reviewed again and again, making sure outputs stayed self-consistent, mathematically sound, and fit for DynamoDB rules along with later-stage ML tools.

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text:
Managing Missing Data
Because the system depends on asynchronous - like OSRM calls, sim-loop state changes, or DynamoDB saves - some data gaps showed up during tests. Missing values were identified through validation rules embedded directly in the backend. If an OSRM call dropped, for instance, the lack of path shape activated a backup straight-line router. Likewise, absent distance or speed values got caught either at truck start-up or while pulling records from DynamoDB later in the cycle.
To tackle these problems, we set up automatic backup options. When coordinates are absent, the system uses direct path estimation - while gaps in speed data fall back on a standard truck rate of 80 km/h. Estimated arrival times get recalculated whenever needed based on leftover distance and adjusted velocity figures. Since processing runs non-stop, no records are deleted; rather, reliable placeholder values keep operations stable. Instead of typical heatmap tools for spotting blanks, our model logs such events directly, noting each time defaults activate - giving engineers clear insight into performance.

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text:
Outlier Detection and Treatment
In simulations, outliers in data often come from math mistakes instead of actual freal-world anomalies. For instance, OSRM might sometimes suggest unusually long route bends; similarly, ship GPS noise can generate positions beyond normal sea zones. To assess these cases, we tracked total distance patterns per planned path while ensuring truck and vessel movements stayed inside typical limits. If sudden big shifts appeared - like a marine unit jumping over half a degree in lat or lon during one reading - the model adjusted those figures to acceptable levels.
Due to outliers affecting plot precision along with model input quality, adjustments are made instead of deletions. During building stages, evaluations resembling box plots confirmed total distance trends rose steadily, while step-by-step gaps stayed inside plausible limits. Such built-in validations stop irregular points from entering outputs meant for display or analysis.

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text:
Data Type Correction and Formatting
A large part of prep work focused on keeping data types uniform throughout the system. Because DynamoDB needs numbers as Decimal objects instead of Python floats, every value for latitude, longitude, distance, or speed was carefully transformed using conditional checks prior to entry. Timestamps like started_at or eta were adjusted into ISO 8601 format through dedicated formatting rules so different parts of the application - backend, frontend, even third-party tools - could reliably use them.
Geospatial data needed precise type adjustments: since OSRM delivers coordinates as [lon, lat], these were restructured into (lat, lon) pairs. Instead of keeping route outputs as dictionary lists, they became standard Python tuples once simulations updated. Consistent format use ensures number-sensitive tasks - like estimating arrival times, gauging leftover distances, or creating machine learning features - run without errors.

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text:
Normalization and Scaling
Even artificial data works better with normalization, particularly in machine learning contexts. Prior to integrating ML predictions into the simulation process, we checked how main inputs - like intended speed, leftover distance, or total advancement - were spread out. Leftover distance, for instance, tends to cluster low early on, then shifts toward higher values nearing destination. So that methods such as K-Means grouping and logistic prediction would run smoothly, we adjusted feature scales via z-scores while training models.
Despite small runtime adjustments in the simulation to reduce extra load, checks ensure inputs stay within normal number limits. During training, visual analysis of data before and after scaling showed extreme values didn’t skew results - either for grouping or labeling patterns.

title: Data Cleaning and Preprocessing
text:
Subsetting the Data
For analysis and modeling, not all simulated fields were necessary. We subset the data to focus on features most relevant to our machine learning objectives:

planned_speed_kmh (continuous)
dist_remaining (continuous)
stop_count (engineered categorical, currently zero in the simulation)
arrival_status (binary classification label for supervised training)

By filtering down to these variables, we reduced dimensionality and ensured that the models learned from data directly tied to operational performance. Additional fields such as raw coordinates, route polyline data, and cumulative distances were retained only for visualization and geospatial logic. This separation allowed the ML models to operate efficiently without being influenced by large, high-granularity geospatial structures.
By filtering down to these variables, we reduced dimensionality while keeping inputs closely linked to real-world operations. Aside from those, details like GPS points, path lines, or total distance stayed in use - but just for maps and location-based functions. Thanks to this split, machine learning tools ran faster, avoiding interference from dense spatial datasets.
The subsetting process preserves a clean distinction between:

High-frequency spatial data (used for the map)
Low-dimensional operational data (used for ML)

This distinction helps keep the ML component lightweight and interpretable while maintaining full simulation fidelity.

title: How to Run the Supply Chain Tracker
text:
This guide explains how to run both the backend API server and the frontend web application.



Python 3.8+ installed
AWS Account with DynamoDB access
AWS Credentials configured (see AWS Setup below)






pip install -r requirements.txt



You need AWS credentials configured to access DynamoDB. You can do this in one of these ways:
Option A: AWS CLI Configuration
aws configure
Enter your AWS Access Key ID, Secret Access Key, and region (eu-north-1).
Option B: Environment Variables
export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=your_access_key
export AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=your_secret_key
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=eu-north-1
Option C: IAM Role (if running on EC2/ECS/Lambda)



The code uses environment variables for DynamoDB configuration. If your table name or region is different, set these:
# Set your DynamoDB table name (default: "Shipments")
export DYNAMODB_TABLE_NAME=YourTableName

# Set your AWS region (default: "eu-north-1")
export AWS_REGION=your-region
# OR
export AWS_DEFAULT_REGION=your-region
Table Requirements: - Primary Key: truckId (String type) - The code will work with your existing table if it has this primary key structure
If you need to create a new table:
aws dynamodb create-table \
    --table-name Shipments \
    --attribute-definitions AttributeName=truckId,AttributeType=S \
    --key-schema AttributeName=truckId,KeyType=HASH \
    --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
    --region eu-north-1






The backend provides the API and WebSocket endpoints for real-time updates.
# Using uvicorn directly
uvicorn server:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload

# Or using Python with uvicorn
python -m uvicorn server:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 --reload
The server will start on http://localhost:8000
Available Endpoints: - GET / - Health check - POST /start-sim - Start a new simulation - WS /ws - WebSocket for real-time updates



Open the HTML files in a web browser:

Setup Page: Open _site/index.html in your browser

Fill in the form to configure your simulation
Click “Start Simulation”

Live Map: After starting simulation, you’ll be redirected to _site/simulate.html

This page connects to the WebSocket and displays real-time updates


Note: If you’re opening HTML files directly (file://), you may need to run a local web server:
# Using Python's built-in server
cd _site
python -m http.server 8080

# Then open in browser: http://localhost:8080/index.html



If you prefer the Streamlit interface:
streamlit run app.py
This will open at http://localhost:8501





Terminal 1 - Start Backend:
uvicorn server:app --reload --port 8000
Terminal 2 - Start Frontend Server (optional, for HTML files):
cd _site
python -m http.server 8080
Open Browser:

Go to http://localhost:8080/index.html (or open _site/index.html directly)
Fill out the form:

Number of trucks: 4
Origin: Basra Port
Destination: Baghdad Depot
Departure time: (any datetime)

Click “Start Simulation”
You’ll be redirected to the live map showing trucks moving in real-time








Verify AWS credentials are set correctly
Check that the Shipments table exists in eu-north-1 region
Ensure your AWS user/role has DynamoDB read/write permissions




If port 8000 is already in use, change it:
uvicorn server:app --port 8001
Then update the frontend JavaScript to use http://localhost:8001 instead.




Make sure the backend server is running
Check browser console for errors
Verify CORS settings if accessing from a different origin




Make sure all dependencies are installed:
pip install -r requirements.txt




For production, consider: - Using environment variables for AWS credentials - Setting up proper CORS origins instead of ["*"] - Using a production ASGI server like Gunicorn with uvicorn workers - Setting up proper logging and monitoring
